input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Explain the assembly process that converts JSON section outputs into a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib, conservative validation checks applied (schema, citation coverage, unsupported-claim detection), and documented failure modes with remediation steps (e.g., re-retrieval, re-generation, manual audit).

output:
The assembly stage converts validated, JSON-constrained section outputs into a compilable LaTeX manuscript and an accompanying refs.bib file.  We organize this stage as a deterministic transformation pipeline that (1) maps JSON fields to LaTeX structural commands, (2) collects and deduplicates bibliographic entries, and (3) emits a top-level TeX wrapper that preserves section order derived from the document graph.  The mapping is intentionally conservative: free-text fields become paragraph bodies, ``section_title'' fields become \texttt{\textbackslash section} or \texttt{\textbackslash subsection} commands according to the node depth, and an explicit ``citations'' array in each JSON node drives insertion of \texttt{\textbackslash cite\{\}} tokens adjacent to the quoted or asserted text. (General background knowledge.)

Assembly follows a small set of implementation rules to keep the resulting artifact audit-friendly and easy to edit by humans:
- Maintain one canonical BibTeX record per cited source and reference it by stable keys generated from JSON provenance metadata. (General background knowledge.)
- Preserve provenance metadata from each JSON node (retrieval queries, evidence snippet identifiers, generation timestamp, and model configuration) in an appendix or in JSON comments alongside the LaTeX source so that later audits can trace every assertion back to its inputs. (General background knowledge.)
- Emit minimal, well-formed LaTeX that compiles with standard toolchains; where complex macros are required, document them in a single preamble include file rather than scattering custom formatting across sections. (General background knowledge.)

Validation is applied at two granularities before final assembly: syntactic/schema-level checks and conservative evidence-aware audits. Schema validation ensures that each section JSON satisfies required fields (for example, title, body, and a non-empty citations list when applicable). Evidence-aware audits apply heuristic checks intended to flag unsupported claims rather than to prove truthfulness. Typical audits include:
- Citation coverage check: verify that any sentence annotated as containing a factual assertion is associated with one or more cited sources in the JSON. (General background knowledge.)
- BibTeX consistency check: confirm that every cited key in the LaTeX body is present in refs.bib and that refs.bib contains only well-formed entries. (General background knowledge.)
- Unsupported-claim detection heuristics: flag sentences with assertive predicates and numeric facts that lack attached evidence metadata for human review. (General background knowledge.)

When a validation check fails, the pipeline records structured failure artifacts (error type, affected section node key, and the offending JSON fragment) and applies a prioritized remediation policy. Common failure modes and associated remediations are:
- Missing or malformed fields in JSON (schema violation): reject the section and enqueue it for re-generation under a stricter JSON-enforcement prompt; preserve the original JSON and failure log for manual inspection.
- Incomplete citation coverage (e.g., assertions without linked evidence): attempt automated re-retrieval using the section's stored retrieval seed and expanded queries; if re-retrieval returns no high-confidence snippets, mark the claim as requiring manual audit and optionally replace the sentence with an explicit caveat placeholder in the assembled LaTeX. (General background knowledge.)
- Absent or malformed BibTeX entries: attempt deterministic reconstruction of BibTeX metadata from stored provenance (e.g., title, authors, venue); if reconstruction is unreliable, de-duplicate conflicting records and present a shortlist to a human editor. (General background knowledge.)
- Hallucinated or internally inconsistent content (detected via contradiction heuristics or reviewer feedback): isolate the offending subtree in the document graph, re-run leaf-first generation for dependent nodes with injected corrections, and annotate changed material in the assembly output for traceability. (General background knowledge.)

All remediation actions are logged and surfaced to downstream reviewers so that the assembled manuscript remains auditable. In particular, every automated change to a section is accompanied by (a) the prior JSON version, (b) the reparative action taken (e.g., re-retrieval, regeneration with stricter prompt), and (c) a short rationale derived from the validation rule that triggered the change. (General background knowledge.)

Limitations. The procedures above are described at a conceptual and procedural level; we do not provide empirical claims about their effectiveness within this section. The conservative design intentionally favors human-in-the-loop remediation for cases where automated retrieval and validation cannot establish sufficient provenance for an asserted fact. Future work should quantify the trade-offs between automation and manual auditing across larger, publicly shared corpora. (General background knowledge.)
